focus: Three-way Central Texas comparison: Bignoniaceae vs Plantaginaceae/Penstemon vs Acanthaceae
comparison_rule: Do not stop at opposite leaves + tubular/bilabiate flower. Move to habit, leaf architecture, staminodes, and especially fruit/seed morphology.

Bignoniaceae.where_to_look_first: Ask whether the plant is woody and inspect the leaves; local members are vines/trees/shrubs with opposite leaves, often compound. Then find the long capsule and flat winged seeds.
core_characters: Trees, shrubs or lianas; herbs rare.
Leaves usually opposite and often compound; stipules absent.
Flowers showy, tubular/campanulate, usually zygomorphic.
Typically 4 didynamous fertile stamens plus a staminode.
Ovary superior.
Fruit commonly a 2-valved capsule.
Seeds numerous, flattened and commonly winged.
Bignoniaceae.best_tie_breaker: Woody habit + long bivalved capsule + many flat winged seeds.

Plantaginaceae.where_to_look_first: On Penstemon, look inside the flower: four fertile stamens plus the distinctive sterile fifth stamen (staminode/beardtongue), then confirm the ordinary many-seeded capsule.
core_characters: Mostly herbs; leaves simple, opposite or alternate, stipules absent.
Corolla fused, commonly zygomorphic and bilabiate.
Usually 2 or 4 fertile stamens; staminodes may occur.
Penstemon characteristically has 4 fertile stamens plus 1 staminode.
Ovary superior, 2-carpellate with axile placentation.
Fruit usually a many-seeded capsule.
No Acanthaceae retinacula.
Plantaginaceae.best_tie_breaker: Herbaceous Penstemon + 4 fertile stamens + prominent sterile beardtongue/staminode + ordinary capsule.

Acanthaceae.where_to_look_first: If fruit is available, open the capsule: seeds are often held on woody hook-like retinacula/jaculators. That character is far stronger than flower shape.
core_characters: Herbs, shrubs or climbers; leaves usually opposite and simple; stipules absent.
Stems often angular or swollen above nodes; cystoliths often present.
Flowers tubular, often zygomorphic/bilabiate.
Stamens usually 2 or 4(5), sometimes with staminodes.
Ovary superior and typically 2-locular.
Fruit usually a 2-locular loculicidal capsule, often explosively dehiscent.
Seeds are commonly cradled on hook-like retinacula arising from the funicle.
Acanthaceae.best_tie_breaker: Explosive capsule + retinacula/hooks under the seeds.
Acanthaceae.ecology_note: Ruellia ciliatiflora fruits can explosively launch seeds, and published biomechanics studies describe woody retinacula guiding seed release.

quick_key: Woody vine/tree/shrub + opposite often compound leaves + long capsule + flat winged seeds → Bignoniaceae.
Herb + Penstemon-type flower + 4 fertile stamens + sterile beardtongue/staminode + ordinary capsule → Plantaginaceae.
Opposite simple leaves + capsule with seed-launching retinacula/hooks → Acanthaceae.
If fruit is unavailable, keep the ID provisional rather than using tubular flower color alone.

priority_cards.look_here_first: Confirm a woody climbing vine with opposite pinnately compound leaves; then look for the long capsule and thin winged seeds.
confirm: Four fertile stamens plus one staminode.

priority_cards.look_here_first: Do not let the willow-like simple leaves fool you: confirm the large tubular flower and then the long narrow capsule full of winged seeds.
confirm: Shrub/small tree rather than willow-family member.
Leaves simple and narrow, showing that Bignoniaceae is not always compound-leaved.
Long narrow capsule with numerous winged seeds.
priority_cards.note: Useful exception card so learners do not overgeneralize 'Bignoniaceae = compound leaves.'

priority_cards.look_here_first: Look inside the large bilabiate flower for four fertile stamens and the sterile fifth stamen/staminode; then confirm a dry capsule.
confirm: Leaves simple and opposite in the local plant.
Four fertile stamens; Penstemon also carries a sterile fifth stamen (staminode/beardtongue).
Fruit is a capsule opening along lines of dehiscence.
